text:
alex wu: Quick sync — I'm seeing a p95 spike when we switch kernel selection to prefer int8 kernels in the replay harness. TTFT goes up ~12% but TPOT improves slightly. Anyone else?
priya rao: hmm, is the replay using the same KV-cache warmup as the synth run? if cache coldness differs p95 can behave weirdly.
ben li: Confirmed repro on my end. Replay trace had more long-prefix requests so the KV cache warmed differently. p95 jump concentrated on sequences > 512 tokens.
marco gomez: Important to be explicit: our apples->apples rule should be same initial KV state, same batching window, same kernel policy, and identical seed for RNG in the harness. Otherwise TTFT/TPOT comparisons lie.
casey: Agreed. Also worth separating two questions: 1) latency-first metric (TTFT/p95) and 2) steady token throughput (TPOT/goodput). They react to different factors (kernel choice vs batch packing).
priya rao: can we get perf-bot to post a short profile for the failing run? specifically kernel times, batching distribution, and kv cache hit rate breakdown.
perf-bot: Profiling summary (run 2167890123-replay):
```
- kernel A (fp16): median per-step 2.8ms
- kernel B (int8-quant): median per-step 2.2ms but slower first-step due to packing: +1.0ms
- batching windows: 16ms target, actual mean pack=5 reqs, tail 95th=12 reqs
- KV cache hit-rate: 78% overall, 52% on long-prefix flows
- TTFT p95 = 42ms (baseline 37ms), TPOT steady token = 4.1ms/token (baseline 4.3ms)
```
liang zhao: The "slower first-step" for int8 kernel is probably a cold-path barrier: data reformat + quantized kernel init for long sequences. That hurts TTFT.
ben li: So kernel-int8 wins in TPOT but loses on TTFT for many requests. For low-latency workloads we should prefer fp16 or hybrid routing.
alex wu: Proposal: For apples-to-apples bench run we add a two-phase harness: warmup phase (replay N requests to prefill KV), then measurement phase. Also run with fixed batching window and fixed kernel-policy env var.
priya rao: +1. Also add metric definitions to the thread so ops and benchers use same names: TTFT = time from request arrived at runtime to first token emitted (includes scheduling + kernel first-step). TPOT = average time per emitted token after first token (steady-state per-token latency). Goodput = tokens/sec that satisfied SLO (i.e., produced under x ms per token), QPS = request completions/sec.
marco gomez: And note p95/p99 for TTFT vs TPOT: compute both over request-first-token times and per-token times respectively. For goodput vs QPS include both observed and effective (post-backpressure) numbers.
casey: I'll draft an experiment checklist:
```
- baseline: fp16 kernel policy + replay with warmup=500 reqs
- alt1: int8 policy + same warmup
- alt2: hybrid routing: prefer fp16 for short seqs, int8 for long seqs
- measure: TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95, QPS, goodput (tokens/sec under per-token SLO=6ms)
- collect: kernel profiles, batching histogram, KV-hit heatmap, perf counters
```
liang zhao: One extra: lock RNG seed and ensure network jitter noise low (run isolated hosts) — replay harness has a --deterministic flag for this.
perf-bot: Scheduled runs: 2167891000 (baseline), 2167892000 (int8), 2167893000 (hybrid). I'll post results.
alex wu: Great. After runs, we'll reconvene and decide if runtime should do per-request kernel routing (based on prefix length + cache state) or keep static policies. Thanks all :rocket:
